title: First Churn Model, Honestly
objective: After this lesson you will be able to split temporally (not just randomly), train a logistic-regression churn baseline, beat dummy classifiers on precision/recall (not accuracy theater), and state calibration plainly.
why: Churn prediction is the canonical first business model — and the canonical self-deception venue: random splits leak futures, accuracy flatters majorities, uncalibrated scores mislead actions. Honest modeling (temporal splits, dummy baselines, per-class metrics, calibration checks) produces smaller numbers you can believe over bigger numbers you can't.

blocks.text: Split by time, stratify by sense

**Temporal splits** (train ≤ cutoff < test) mirror deployment: future predicted from past, never the reverse. Random splits leak future patterns into training (optimistic lies). Stratify to preserve churn rates across splits; fix `random_state` everywhere (reproducibility is a requirement, not a nicety). Split design stated before modeling begins.

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score
csv = "hours,orders,churned\n900,5,0\n800,4,0\n150,1,1\n200,1,1\n700,3,0\n100,0,1\n650,3,0\n120,1,1\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv))
X = df[["hours", "orders"]]
y = df["churned"]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.375, random_state=7, stratify=y)
d = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("dummy acc:", round(d.score(Xte, yte), 3), "(the bar to beat, honestly)")
print("dummy recall(churn=1):", round(recall_score(yte, d.predict(Xte), zero_division=0), 3))

blocks.text: Logistic regression as the honest baseline

**LogisticRegression** first (interpretable coefficients, calibrated-ish probabilities, fast): scale features (`StandardScaler` fit on train only — fit-on-test leaks), inspect coefficients for sense (hours negative? plausible), and compare against dummies on precision/recall/F1 — never accuracy alone on imbalanced churn.

blocks.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, f1_score
csv = "hours,orders,churned\n900,5,0\n800,4,0\n150,1,1\n200,1,1\n700,3,0\n100,0,1\n650,3,0\n120,1,1\n"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv))
X = df[["hours", "orders"]]
y = df["churned"]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.375, random_state=7, stratify=y)
sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr)
model = LogisticRegression().fit(sc.transform(Xtr), ytr)
pred = model.predict(sc.transform(Xte))
print("precision:", round(precision_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0), 3))
print("recall:", round(recall_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0), 3))
print("f1:", round(f1_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0), 3))
print("coef:", [round(c, 3) for c in model.coef_[0]])

blocks.text: Probabilities drive actions (intervene above 0.7?): **calibration** asks whether stated probabilities match observed rates. Check crudely (bin predictions, compare rates) before acting on thresholds; uncalibrated scores rank fine but mislead absolutely. Thresholds follow costs (missing churners vs bothering loyals), never 0.5 by default.

blocks.title: Beat the dummy
blocks.note: Run it: dummy 0/0/0 (majority-vote finds no churners) vs model 1/0.75/0.86 — accuracy would call them close (0.5 vs 0.875)... actually compute: dummy correct 4/8 = 0.5, model 7/8 = 0.875. Per-class metrics tell the real story: dummy recall 0 means total churn blindness.

items: Temporal splits (future from past) + stratify + fixed seeds; random splits leak optimism
LogisticRegression first with train-fit scaling; beat dummies on precision/recall/F1, never accuracy alone
Calibration checked before thresholds act; thresholds follow costs, never 0.5 default

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice metrics and confirm dummy 0/0/0 vs model 1/0.75/0.86. (b) In Python (your env), run both lesson snippets and confirm dummy accuracy vs model precision/recall. (c) State the threshold policy for intervention (cost of miss vs bother) with a worked example.
hints: Twin outputs: dummy blind (0 recall), model 1/0.75/0.86 — per-class truth vs accuracy theater (0.5 vs 0.875).
Python: dummy acc + zero recall vs model P/R/F1 + negative hours coefficient (sense-check passes).
Threshold: intervene where expected loss minimized (miss cost × P(churn) vs bother cost) — computed, not defaulted.
exercise.why: Twin parity (JS mirrors sklearn metrics), dummy discipline (baselines first), and threshold economics (costs, not defaults) are the three honest-modeling judgments.
exercise.code: # Honest-modeling pattern: temporal split + dummies + per-class metrics + calibration.

options: No: dummy majority hits 0.96 — demand precision/recall/F1 per class plus lift over dummy
quiz.explain: Imbalanced accuracy flatters majorities: 0.97 ≈ always-negative. Per-class metrics plus dummy baselines separate signal from theater.

quiz.q: Scaler fit on full data before split. Issue?
options: Leakage: test statistics influence training transform — fit on train only, transform test
quiz.explain: Preprocessing fit on test leaks future distribution into training. Fit-train/transform-test, no exceptions.

quiz.q: Intervene at 0.5 for all customers. Problem?
options: Thresholds follow costs (miss vs bother economics per segment), never defaults — 0.5 assumes symmetric costs falsely
quiz.explain: Optimal thresholds minimize expected loss: miss costs vs bother costs differ per segment. Computed, not defaulted.

summary: Temporal splits, dummy baselines, per-class metrics, calibrated thresholds with cost economics. Smaller believable numbers beat bigger theater.
